# Future directions

Conjectures suggested by the formalisation in `Catalog/Shared/GilbertLattice*.lean`
of the conditioned Gilbert model (one point per cell of `ℤ²`, two points joined when
their Euclidean distance is `< R`).  Notation as in `GilbertLatticeCriticalRadii.lean`:

* `Rmin  = sInf {R : some placement has an infinite component}` — proved: `1/3 ≤ Rmin ≤ 1/2`;
* `Rconn = sInf {R : some placement connects all the points}` — proved: `1/3 ≤ Rconn ≤ 1`;
* `Rfull = sInf {R : every placement connects all the points}` — proved: `√17/2 ≤ Rfull ≤ √5`.

Each conjecture below is falsifiable by exhibiting one explicit configuration (for the
upper-bound direction) or one explicit infinite path (for the lower-bound direction).

## Conjecture 1 (sharp geometric threshold): `Rmin = 1/2`

Equivalently: for every `R ≤ 1/2` and every placement of the points, all connected
components are finite.  The upper bound `Rmin ≤ 1/2` is proved (the line configuration
`lineConfig`); the formalised lower bound is only `Rmin ≥ 1/3`.  Evidence: an exhaustive
convex optimisation over all periodic drifting paths of period `≤ 4`, and a random
search for periods `5 … 8`, never produced a longest edge below `1/2`
(`ComputationalEvidence.md`).  *Falsifiable*: a periodic path of some period `T` with
nonzero drift and all edges `< 1/2` would refute it.

Proof strategy suggested by the formalisation: along a path each step crosses exactly
one grid line up to bounces (`cross_x`, `cross_y`, and the "no two consecutive steps of
the same type" arguments used in `no_double_x_trivial` / `no_double_y_trivial`), so the
signed slack `a_t = x_t - K_t` to the last vertical line crossed decreases by at least
`1 - 2R` at each column advance.  What is missing for the sharp result is a joint
`x`/`y` potential controlling the recharging of the slack by direction reversals.

## Conjecture 2 (quantitative subcriticality): exponentially small components below `1/2`

For every `R < 1/2` there are constants `c(R), C(R) > 0` such that, for **every**
placement, the component of a given cell has at most `C(R)` cells, with
`C(R) = O((1-2R)^{-2})` as `R ↑ 1/2`.  The formalised result gives `C(R) = 9` for
`R < 1/3` (`component_finite`, in fact components lie in a `3 × 3` block).  The slack
recursion `a_{t+1} ≤ a_t - (1-2R)` suggests a diameter of order `1/(1-2R)` in each
coordinate.  *Falsifiable*: a family of placements whose components have diameter
growing faster than `(1-2R)^{-1}` in some coordinate.

## Conjecture 3 (full connectivity): `Rfull = √5`

Every placement is connected as soon as `R > √5` (proved), and we conjecture that this
is optimal: for every `R < √5` there is a placement whose graph is disconnected.  Our
verified lower bound is only `√17/2 ≈ 2.0616`, obtained from a *straight* horizontal cut
with a `1/2` horizontal stagger.  A refutation would be a proof that every placement is
connected for some `R < √5` — e.g. showing that the worst cut is the straight staggered
one, which would instead give `Rfull = √17/2`.  Deciding between `√17/2` and `√5` (or an
intermediate value coming from a periodic wavy cut) is a concrete finite-dimensional
optimisation over cut shapes.

## Conjecture 4 (connected placements): `Rconn = 1`

The centred placement connects all points for `R > 1` (proved: `centerConfig_connected`),
and we conjecture no placement does better: for `R ≤ 1`, every placement has at least one
point isolated from the rest, i.e. the graph is never connected.  Intuition: to connect
*all* points, in particular the four points of every `2 × 2` block, the placement cannot
be compressed onto lines, and one unit of "grid spacing" must be paid somewhere.
*Falsifiable*: a placement (periodic, say) with all points connected and all edges of a
spanning structure `< 1`.

## Conjecture 5 (probabilistic threshold): `1/2 < R_c < √5`, with `R_c` non-degenerate

For the random model (each point uniform in its cell, independently), let `R_c` be the
almost sure percolation threshold.  Then `Rmin ≤ R_c` and `R_c ≤ √5`, both of which
follow from the results formalised here (below `Rmin` no placement percolates; above
`√5` every placement is connected).  We conjecture the strict inequalities
`Rmin = 1/2 < R_c < √5`, and more precisely that `R_c` is strictly larger than the
threshold `R'` at which the two-row line mechanism becomes available, because that
mechanism has probability zero in the random model.  *Falsifiable*: a proof that
`R_c = 1/2`, or a numerical simulation exhibiting an infinite cluster for `R` close to
`1/2`.  A first formalisable step is a rigorous, computer-checkable bound of the form
`R_c ≥ R₀` obtained by a Peierls contour argument on the induced dependent bond
percolation on `ℤ²`.

# Future directions

Derived from the results now proved in `Catalog/Shared/DreamRevisionNormalForm.lean`
(last-occurrence normalization `mem_reviseSeq`, extensional rigidity `reviseSeq_ext_iff`,
normal-form uniqueness up to permutation `normalForm_unique`, the frame property
`persistent_nonexplosion`, and the component classification `mutually_reachable_iff`).

## 1. The revision monoid is the free "last-write-wins" monoid

**Conjecture.** The map sending a history `ls` to its action `B ↦ reviseSeq B ls` is a
monoid homomorphism from `List (Literal Atom)` (concatenation) onto the monoid of partial
sign assignments `Atom →₀ Option Bool` under *right-biased overwrite*, and its kernel
congruence is generated by exactly the two local rules `revise_comm_of_ne_atom` and
`revise_revise_of_eq_atom`.

*Falsifiable content.* Produce two histories with the same action that cannot be connected
by a finite chain of the two local rewrites. `reviseSeq_ext_iff` already shows that the
action is determined by `lastSign`, so the open half is completeness of the rewrite system;
`normalForm_unique` supplies the confluence target.

## 2. Component geometry: cube structure, diameter, and orientation

**Conjecture.** For a finite atom set `A`, the strongly connected component of the revision
graph indexed by an assigned set `S ⊆ A` is isomorphic (as a graph with self-loops removed)
to the `|S|`-dimensional hypercube graph `Q_{|S|}`, so it has `2^{|S|}` vertices and
diameter `|S|`; the whole revision graph is the disjoint union of these cubes together with
the strictly monotone edges that enlarge `S`, and its condensation is order-isomorphic to
the Boolean lattice `2^A`.

*Falsifiable content.* Exhibit a component that is not a cube, or a pair of states in one
component whose revision distance exceeds `|S|`. `mutually_reachable_iff` fixes the vertex
sets of the components; the metric statement is untouched so far.

## 3. Optimal-length histories and a normal-form metric

**Conjecture.** For consistent finite states `B, C` with `assigned B ⊆ assigned C`, the
minimal length of a history `ls` with `reviseSeq B ls = C` equals `|C \ B|`, and any minimal
history is a permutation of the list of literals of `C \ B`.

*Falsifiable content.* A pair `B, C` reachable by a strictly shorter history than
`|C \ B|`. The construction in `reachable_of_assigned_eq` gives the upper bound `|C|`; the
sharpened bound and the rigidity of minimizers are open.

## 4. Failure of the frame property for non-local revision operators

**Conjecture.** Among all operators `r : Set (Literal Atom) → Literal Atom →
Set (Literal Atom)` satisfying "success" (`l ∈ r B l`) and "consistency preservation",
`revise` is the unique one satisfying the frame law of `reviseSeq_frame`
(`p.1 ≠ l.1 → (p ∈ r B l ↔ p ∈ B)`); equivalently, the frame law plus success characterizes
`revise` outright, with consistency preservation a consequence rather than an assumption.

*Falsifiable content.* A second operator with success and the frame law that differs from
`revise` on some state — necessarily differing only in whether `opposite l` is retracted.

## 5. Ideal completion of finite states and continuity of revision

**Conjecture.** The poset of finite signed states, ordered by inclusion, has ideal
completion order-isomorphic to all signed states, the isomorphism restricts to consistent
ideals ↔ consistent states, and `reviseSeq` is Scott-continuous in the state argument: for
every directed family `{B_i}`, `reviseSeq (⋃ B_i) ls = ⋃ reviseSeq B_i ls`.

*Falsifiable content.* The continuity half is immediately testable from `mem_reviseSeq`,
since membership in `reviseSeq B ls` depends on `B` only through membership of the single
point `p`; a directed family violating the displayed identity would refute it. The harder
half is that the topological identification respects the *consistency* predicate, which is
not Scott-open (it is co-open), so a mismatch would show up exactly at limit points.

# Future directions

The four files in `Catalog/Shared/ZeroKnowledge/` develop, with complete proofs:

* `ThreeColoringZK.lean` — the GMW protocol for graph 3-colorability: perfect
  completeness, the `1 - 1/|E|` soundness gap (shown tight on `K₄`), exponential
  amplification, and **perfect zero knowledge** (the real view distribution is literally
  equal to the witness-free simulator's, hence also witness-indistinguishable).
* `SnarkSoundness.lean` — a simplified zk-SNARK: R1CS arithmetization, the batching
  polynomial, faithfulness, Schwartz–Zippel soundness `(m-1)/|F|`, error amplification,
  algebraic knowledge extraction from `m` distinct challenges, and perfect hiding of a
  one-time-pad field mask.
* `PCPBridge.lean` — the same verifier read as a 2-query PCP: locality, query count,
  the completeness/soundness gap, and an *exact* parallel repetition theorem
  (`accepting k-tuples = accCard ^ k`) with the resulting `2k` queries versus
  `exp(-k/|E|)` error trade-off.
* `NIZKFiatShamir.lean` — non-interactive zero knowledge in the random-oracle model:
  exact fiber counting for uniform oracles (uniformity of `H a`, undetectability of
  reprogramming at one point), the identity `Pr[H a ∈ B] = |B|/|Chal|`, a union bound
  over the prover's choice of first message, and Fiat–Shamir soundness for a
  `d`-special-sound Σ-protocol.

Natural continuations:

1. **Sequential and concurrent composition.** Prove that the perfect-ZK property of
   `viewProb` is preserved under `k`-fold sequential repetition by showing that the
   product view distribution factorizes, i.e. `viewProb^{⊗k} = simProb^{⊗k}`.

2. **Commitment schemes as a first-class object.** The present treatment idealizes the
   commitment (the verifier learns exactly the two opened symbols). Formalizing
   computationally hiding/binding commitments requires a notion of negligible function and
   of efficient adversary; a first step is a statistically hiding, perfectly binding scheme
   over a finite field, where all statements remain finite counting statements.

3. **From special soundness to knowledge soundness.** `batch_extraction` extracts from `m`
   accepting transcripts algebraically. The general rewinding-based extractor (an expected
   polynomial-time argument) would need a probabilistic-complexity layer on top of the
   present counting layer.

4. **Full QAP / Groth16 pipeline.** Convert `R1CS` to a quadratic arithmetic program by
   interpolating the constraint matrices at distinct evaluation points and prove the
   divisibility criterion `A(X)·B(X) - C(X) = H(X)·Z(X)` is equivalent to satisfaction.
   Mathlib's `Lagrange` interpolation API makes this reachable.

5. **Genuine gap amplification for the PCP theorem.** The repetition theorem here increases
   the number of queries. Dinur-style gap amplification keeps the query complexity constant
   at the price of a larger alphabet; formalizing even the graph-powering step (with
   expander mixing, which Mathlib now partially supports) would be a substantial next
   target on the road to `NP ⊆ PCP(log n, O(1))`.

6. **Zero knowledge for the PCP verifier.** Combining `PCPBridge.lean` with the simulator of
   `ThreeColoringZK.lean` should yield a *zero-knowledge PCP*: the verifier's local view of
   the randomized proof string is simulable. The counting lemma `perm3_pair_count`
   generalizes to `k` queries as long as the queried vertices carry pairwise distinct
   colours, which fails in general — quantifying the resulting leakage is an interesting
   combinatorial question.

# Future Directions (thread th_995e2be3)

The thread attacks *quantitative sphere detection from finite data*: which explicitly
computable, perturbation-stable quantities of a finite sample certify the topology of the
underlying space.  Three Lean files carry the formal content; all compile against Mathlib
and contain **no `sorry`** and no added axioms (the theorems depend only on `propext`,
`Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

## Cycle 1 — Direction 3: correspondence-based Rips interleaving

`Catalog/Bridges/GraphTheory/RipsCorrespondenceInterleaving.lean`

1. Rips simplices of a finite sample: monotonicity in the scale, closure under subsets.
2. Correspondences and their **distortion**; existence of choice maps.
3. A choice map of a correspondence of distortion `≤ c` expands distances by at most `c`,
   hence pushes `ε`-Rips simplices to `(ε+c)`-Rips simplices (both directions), i.e. a
   two-sided `c`-interleaving of Rips filtrations.
4. The round trip `g ∘ f` moves points by at most `c`, and `s ∪ (g∘f)(s)` is an
   `(ε+2c)`-simplex — the contiguity that makes the interleaving descend to homology.
5. Distortions add under composition of correspondences.
6. Samples at Hausdorff distance `≤ δ` are related by the `δ`-closeness correspondence, of
   distortion `≤ 2δ`; the resulting `2δ` scale translation is sharp.
7. Matched samples (`dist (X i) (Y i) ≤ δ`) are the special case of an indexwise
   correspondence, recovering the classical `2δ` translation.
8. Sharpness: for every `c > 0` and every shift `η < c` there is a correspondence of
   distortion `≤ c` for which the shift `η` fails.

## Cycle 2 — Directions 4 and 5: link certificates and the guarded interval

`Catalog/Bridges/GraphTheory/RipsLinkGuardedInterval.lean`

Global Betti numbers cannot separate manifolds from singular homology mimics; the mission's
Directions 4 and 5 therefore ask for *local* link data and for an interval-valued detector
with stable endpoints.  This file supplies the quantitative skeleton of both, again as a
chain in which each result uses the previous ones.

1. `ripsBall` / `linkDeg` — the closed vertex star of a sample point and its cardinality.
   `mem_ripsBall_iff_isRipsSimplex` identifies the ball with the set of vertices spanning
   an edge with `v`, so the link degree is an invariant of the Rips complex.
2. `ripsBall_mono`, `linkDeg_mono` — link degrees are monotone in the scale.
3. `IsDeltaMatching`, `dist_map_le`, `le_dist_map` — a `δ`-matching distorts distances by at
   most `2δ`: the local shadow of the distortion bound of cycle 1.
4. `Separated`, `map_injOn` — on an `η`-separated sample with `2δ < η`, a `δ`-matching is
   injective, so it cannot collapse links.  (Randomised search shows the hypothesis is not
   removable: collapsing matchings do destroy link degrees.)
5. `ripsBall_image_subset`, `linkDeg_le_of_matching` — hence
   `linkDeg S ε v ≤ linkDeg T (ε + 2δ) (f v)`.
6. `GuardedAt`, `GuardedAt_mono`, `GuardedAt_perturb`, `GuardedAt_perturb_ray` — the local
   guard "every vertex link has at least `k` vertices" is an up-set in the scale, is
   transported by a `δ`-matching with a `2δ` shift, and then holds on the whole ray.
7. `exists_diam_bound`, `guardedAt_diam`, `guardSet_nonempty`, `guardSet_bddBelow` — the
   guarded interval `guardSet S k` is a nonempty up-set bounded below by `0`, so its left
   endpoint `guardThreshold S k` exists and is nonnegative.
8. `guardThreshold_stability`, `guardThreshold_stability_abs` — **the endpoint of the
   guarded interval is stable**: under a `δ`-matching of an `η`-separated sample with
   `2δ < η`, `|guardThreshold T k − guardThreshold S k| ≤ 2δ`.  This is the Lipschitz
   endpoint stability asked for in Direction 5, for the link-degree guard.
9. `guardSet_pair`, `guardThreshold_pair` — the guarded interval of `{0, r} ⊆ ℝ` at `k = 2`
   is exactly `[r, ∞)`: the guard is not vacuous and the endpoint is computed exactly.
10. `linkDeg_shift_sharp` — the `2δ` shift of step 5 is optimal: for any `η < ε + 2δ` there
    is a `δ`-matching with `linkDeg S ε 0 = 2` but `linkDeg T η (f 0) = 1`.

## Cycle 3 — Direction 2: coverage, packing and the `n^{-1/d}` density law

`Catalog/Bridges/GraphTheory/RipsCoverageDensity.lean`

Cycles 1 and 2 are *scale-free*: they bound how much a detector moves under a `δ`-matching
but say nothing about how large `δ` and the separation `η` may be for a sample of `n`
points.  Direction 2 asks exactly this.  Cycle 3 supplies the deterministic
(measure-theoretic) half of the `n^{-1/d}` law in a finite-dimensional normed space `E`
with an additive Haar measure `μ`, writes `d = finrank ℝ E`, `V = μ K`, `v = μ (ball 0 1)`,
and then feeds the result back into the cycle-2 stability theorem.  Again each result uses
the previous ones.

1. `IsCoverAt P K ρ` — the sample `P` is a `ρ`-cover of `K` (its *resolution* is `ρ`);
   `IsCoverAt.subset_iUnion` turns this into a covering by closed `ρ`-balls.
2. `IsCoverAt.measure_le`, `IsCoverAt.volume_le` — subadditivity plus the Haar scaling law
   `μ (closedBall x ρ) = ρ^d · μ (ball 0 1)` give `V ≤ n · ρ^d · v`.
3. `IsCoverAt.le_card`, `IsCoverAt.le_pow` — hence `n ≥ V/(v ρ^d)` and `ρ^d ≥ V/(v n)`.
4. `IsCoverAt.rpow_le` — **the `n^{-1/d}` law**: `ρ ≥ (V/(v n))^{1/d}`.  No sampling scheme,
   random or not, can have covering radius below this floor.  The `log n` factor of the
   probabilistic coverage threshold is therefore a genuine excess over the deterministic
   floor coming from extreme gaps, not an artefact — which is precisely the correction to
   the "bare power law" that Direction 2 asks for.
5. `packing_card_bound` — dually, an `η`-separated sample (the hypothesis of the cycle-2
   stability theorem) inside a ball of radius `R` satisfies `n · (η/2)^d ≤ (R + η/2)^d`,
   because the open `η/2`-balls around the sample points are disjoint.
6. `separation_le_two_radius`, `packing_spacing_bound`, `packing_spacing_rpow` — hence
   `n · η^d ≤ (4R)^d` and `η · n^{1/d} ≤ 4R`: the *spacing* obeys the same power law, so
   spacing and resolution are governed by the same exponent (a distinction Direction 2 asks
   to keep separate — they differ only in the constant, not in the power).
7. `IsCoverAt.hausdorffLe`, `IsCoverAt.exists_rips_shift`, `rips_shift_floor` — two samples
   of the *same* set `K`, each of resolution `ρ`, are automatically at Hausdorff distance
   `≤ ρ`, so the cycle-1 interleaving applies with shift `2ρ`; and by step 4 that budget can
   never be smaller than `2 (V/(v n))^{1/d}`.  Refining the sample is the only way to shrink
   the interleaving error, and it shrinks only like `n^{-1/d}`.
8. `noise_resolution_tradeoff`, `noise_resolution_tradeoff_rpow` — combining 3 and 6, any
   noise level `δ ≥ 0` admissible for the cycle-2 hypothesis `2δ < η` satisfies
   `V · δ^d ≤ v · (2Rρ)^d`, i.e. `δ · V^{1/d} ≤ 2Rρ · v^{1/d}`.  The sample size has
   cancelled: **the admissible noise is at most a fixed geometric multiple of the
   resolution.**
9. `guardThreshold_shift_le_resolution` — the capstone, which uses cycle 2's
   `RipsGuard.guardThreshold_stability_abs` directly: the shift `Δ` of the left endpoint of
   the guarded interval under a matched `δ`-perturbation satisfies
   `V · |Δ|^d ≤ v · (4Rρ)^d`.  Endpoint stability is thus not merely Lipschitz in `δ`; it is
   controlled by how finely the underlying set has been sampled, uniformly in the number of
   sample points.

## What remains open

* **Persistent homology.**  The cycle-1 and cycle-2 files are simplicial (image, contiguity and link
  statements).  Turning them into statements about persistence modules requires simplicial
  homology of flag/Rips complexes as a functor of the scale, which is not available in the
  library; `Correspondence.union_roundTrip_isRipsSimplex` is precisely the input such a
  functorial argument needs.
* **Gromov–Hausdorff.**  `DistortionLe` gives `2 d_GH(S,T) = inf over correspondences of the
  distortion`; formalising this identity for finite metric spaces would upgrade the
  interleaving to the standard stability theorem.
* **From degree guards to manifold links.**  `GuardedAt` is the crudest link certificate
  (a lower bound on the number of neighbours).  The next step is a combinatorial *link
  complex* `lk(v)` of the flag complex together with a certificate that `lk(v)` has the
  homology of `S^{d−1}`; the perturbation machinery of steps 3–5 (injectivity on separated
  samples, `2δ` shift) should transport such a certificate verbatim, but the homology of the
  link has to be defined first.
* **Guarded Poincaré interval.**  Combining a sphere-homology predicate with the link guard
  requires the homological half; once available, the endpoint-stability argument of step 8
  (an infimum over an up-set that is transported by a `2δ` shift) applies unchanged to the
  conjunction, provided the homological predicate is itself monotone on a persistence gap.
* **Reach and density (Direction 1).**  The interleaving isolates the noise contribution
  exactly; the missing ingredient is a reach-dependent upper endpoint making the interval
  `[2δ, f(τ)]` nonempty.  This needs reach/medial-axis theory, absent from the library.
* **Coverage law (Direction 2), probabilistic layer.**  Cycle 3 settles the deterministic
  floor `ρ ≥ (V/(v n))^{1/d}` and the matching packing bound in a finite-dimensional normed
  space.  What is still missing is the probabilistic layer: matching upper and lower tail
  bounds of order `(log n / n)^{1/d}` for `n` i.i.d. uniform points, with constants uniform
  over a range of dimensions.  The deterministic floor is the lower half of the sandwich;
  the upper half needs a Chernoff/union bound over a `ρ`-net, which in turn needs a
  covering-number estimate for the sphere (available in the library only in the abstract
  totally-bounded form).
* **Curved ambient spaces.**  Cycle 3 uses the exact Haar scaling `μ(B(x,ρ)) = ρ^d μ(B(0,1))`,
  valid in a normed space.  On a compact submanifold of reach `≥ τ` the same argument runs
  with two-sided Bishop–Gromov-type volume comparison `c ρ^d ≤ μ(B(x,ρ)) ≤ C ρ^d` for
  `ρ ≤ τ`; isolating that comparison as a hypothesis (rather than proving it) would extend
  every statement of cycle 3 verbatim and connect Direction 2 to Direction 1.
* **Sharp constants.**  `packing_card_bound` loses a factor `2^d` on the way to
  `packing_spacing_bound`, and the capstone constant `4Rρ` is certainly not optimal.  The
  sharp constants are the sphere/ball packing and covering densities, which are not in the
  library.

# Future Directions

Conjectures suggested by the formalization in `Catalog/Bridges/VertexSplitting.lean` and
`Catalog/Bridges/VertexSplittingExact.lean`.
All are stated in the vocabulary of those files (`IsSplit`, `IsExclusive`, `IsProjExclusive`,
`SplitChain`, `IsCograph`, `IsChordal`, `IsPtFree`, `HasUnitIntervalRep`, `HasInducedClaw`,
`matchingGraph`, `starGraph`).

Throughout, `split_Π(G)` denotes the minimum of `|W| − |V|` over all `H : SimpleGraph W`
and `f : W → V` with `IsSplit G H f` and `Π H`.

## Resolved in this project

* Every splitting map factors into single `singleSplit` steps, and the factorization can be taken
  shallow: `exists_singleSplit_factor`, `SplitChain.of_isSplit`, `splitChain_matchingGraph`.
  Consequently, in this model shallowness costs nothing.
* Unit interval graphs are chordal: `isChordal_of_unitIntervalRep`.  Hence
  `split_IsChordal(G) ≤ split_HasUnitIntervalRep(G)` for every `G`.
* Exact splitting numbers of the smallest obstructions:
  `split_IsCograph(P₄) = 1` (`cograph_split_pathP4_exact`),
  `split_IsChordal(C₄) = 1` (`chordal_split_cycleC4_exact`),
  `split_HasUnitIntervalRep(K_{1,3}) = split_HasUnitIntervalRep(K_{1,4}) = 1`
  (`unitInterval_split_starK13_exact`, `unitInterval_split_starK14_exact`).
  In each case the optimal split can be taken exclusive.
* **A conjecture of the previous iteration was refuted.**  It was conjectured that
  `split_HasUnitIntervalRep(K_{1,n}) = n − 2`.  In fact pairing up the leaves gives
  `split_HasUnitIntervalRep(K_{1,n}) = ⌈n/2⌉ − 1` for every `n ≥ 1`
  (`unitInterval_split_star_exact`), with a matching lower bound valid for every claw-free target
  (`card_ge_of_split_clawFree_star`).  For `n = 4` the true value is `1`, not `2`.

## Conjectures

1. **Exclusive splittings need not decompose into exclusive single splits.**
   `SplitChain.of_isSplit` produces an *exclusive* chain (each `singleSplit` step has
   `A ∩ B = ∅`) from the hypothesis `IsProjExclusive H f`, which is strictly stronger than
   `IsExclusive H f`.  Conjecture: there are finite `G, H, f` with `IsSplit G H f` and
   `IsExclusive H f` for which **no** chain `SplitChain True G H f` exists — i.e. the ordering
   of splits genuinely matters for exclusivity, and `IsProjExclusive` is the right invariant.
   Falsifiable by proving `IsExclusive H f → SplitChain True G H f` in general.

2. **No exclusivity gap for cograph splitting.**
   (Exclusivity is automatic when the target has maximum degree at most one —
   `isExclusive_of_deg_le_one` — and all optimal splits computed in this project are exclusive.)
   For every finite graph `G`, the minimum number of splits producing a cograph equals the
   minimum number of *exclusive* splits producing a cograph.
   Falsifiable by a graph whose exclusive cograph splitting number is strictly larger than its
   unrestricted one.

3. **A cyclomatic bound for chordal targets.**
   For every finite `G`, `split_IsChordal(G) ≤ |E| − |V| + c(G)`, where `c(G)` is the number of
   connected components; i.e. one split per independent cycle suffices.  The case of a single
   cycle is proved for `C₄` (`chordal_split_cycleC4_exact`), where unfolding the cycle at one
   vertex produces the path `P₅` (`isSplit_pathP5_cycleC4`).  Falsifiable by a graph needing more
   splits than its cyclomatic number.

4. **A local degree lower bound for claw-free (hence unit interval) targets.**
   For every finite `G`, every splitting of `G` into a claw-free graph has at least
   `Σ_v ⌈deg(v)/2⌉` vertices coming from vertices of degree at least one, so
   `split_HasUnitIntervalRep(G) ≥ Σ_v (⌈deg(v)/2⌉ − 1)`.
   This is exactly `card_ge_of_split_clawFree_star` when `G` is a star, where it is tight.
   Falsifiable by a graph and a claw-free splitting violating the count.

5. **Hereditary monotonicity under induced subgraphs.**
   If `Π` is hereditary (closed under induced subgraphs) then `split_Π(G') ≤ split_Π(G)` for
   every induced subgraph `G'` of `G`; in particular this holds for `IsCograph`, `IsPtFree t`,
   `IsChordal` and `HasUnitIntervalRep`.  Falsifiable by an induced subgraph that needs strictly
   more splits than the whole graph, for one of these classes.

# Future directions: falsifiable conjectures from the group-model Schnorr formalization

The new files are

* `Catalog/Cryptography/ZeroKnowledge/SchnorrGroupProtocol.lean` — Schnorr Σ-protocol in a
  commutative group of exponent `q` (`gexp` API, completeness, knowledge soundness /
  extraction, perfect HVZK as an equality of `PMF`s, soundness error `≤ 1/q`);
* `Catalog/Cryptography/ZeroKnowledge/SchnorrGroupFiatShamir.lean` — the Fiat–Shamir
  transform, forking extraction, oracle programming, and the random-oracle bounds `1/q` and
  `Q/q`;
* `Catalog/Cryptography/ZeroKnowledge/SchnorrGroupInstances.lean` — exact soundness error
  `= 1/q` in a cyclic group of prime order, unique responses, and the concrete instance
  `Multiplicative (ZMod q)`;
* `Catalog/Cryptography/ZeroKnowledge/SchnorrGroupBridge.lean` — identification of the
  catalog's additive model (`Cryptography.SchnorrIdentification`) with the group model at
  `Multiplicative (ZMod p)`, plus the resulting `PMF`-level HVZK statement for the additive
  model.

Each conjecture below is a precise Lean-statable claim that can be proved or refuted.

## C1. The `Q/q` random-oracle bound is tight, and `Q/q` is attained only by distinct commitments

`rom_union_bound` shows that an adversary precommitting to `Q` pairs `(a i, z i)` succeeds
with probability at most `Q/q` over the oracle answer vector.  Conjecture: in a cyclic group
of prime order `q`, equality holds **iff** the commitments `a i` are pairwise distinct (and
`Q ≤ q`); if two indices share a commitment, the success probability drops by at least
`1/q²`.  Falsifiable: exhibit a family with repeated commitments attaining `Q/q`.

## C2. Perfect HVZK survives adaptive challenge choice but not adaptive statement choice

`hvzk_pmf` fixes the challenge `c` before sampling.  Conjecture: for every function
`C : G → ZMod q` (a verifier choosing the challenge from the commitment), the honest
transcript distribution `r ↦ (g^r, C (g^r), r + C(g^r)·x)` is **not** in general equal to any
witness-free simulator's output distribution — concretely, there exists `q`, `x` and `C` for
which no simulator matching `hvzk` exists, while for every *constant* `C` one does.  This
would formally separate honest-verifier ZK from malicious-verifier ZK inside the catalog's
framework.

## C3. Special soundness is equivalent to the `1/q` soundness error in this model

Conjecture: for a fixed public key `pub ≠ 1` in a group of prime order `q`, the following are
equivalent for the predicate `Accepts g pub`: (i) any two accepting transcripts with a common
commitment and distinct challenges determine a unique extracted exponent; (ii) for every
`(a, z)` the accepting-challenge set has cardinality exactly one.  We proved (ii) ⇒ tight
soundness error; the converse direction, stated as an abstract property of an arbitrary
acceptance predicate `P : G → ZMod q → ZMod q → Prop`, is open in the formalization and is
the natural definition of a "generic Σ-protocol with knowledge error `1/q`".

## C4. Exponent-`q` hypothesis can be weakened to `pub ∈ Subgroup.zpowers g`

All extraction results assume `pub ^ q = 1`.  Conjecture: `special_soundness_witness` remains
true, with the same extractor, under the strictly weaker hypothesis
`pub ∈ Subgroup.zpowers g` in an arbitrary (possibly infinite, possibly non-commutative but
with `g` central) group, provided `orderOf g = q`.  Falsifiable: a group, `g` of order `q`,
and `pub` a power of `g` for which the extractor fails.

## C5. Fiat–Shamir with commitment-only hashing is insecure for multi-message signing

`FSAccepts` hashes `(pub, a, m)`.  Conjecture: if the message is dropped from the hash input
(oracle of the form `H : G × G → ZMod q`), then there is an explicit adversary that, given a
single valid signature on `m₀`, produces a valid signature on every message `m`, i.e.
universal forgery with probability `1`; whereas with the message included, the `Q/q` bound of
`rom_union_bound` continues to hold.  This is a concrete, checkable separation between the
two hashing conventions inside the present formalization.

# Future directions

The formalisation in `Catalog/Pythagorean/BrillNoether/` now consists of ten
self-contained files, each compiling on its own against Mathlib with no `sorry` and
using only the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.

## What is formalised

* `Divisors.lean` — divisors, linear equivalence, the Baker–Norine rank inequality,
  genus and canonical divisor (`deg K = 2g − 2`), and the mechanism turning an
  `ℓ^∞` covering bound `ρ` for the Laplacian lattice into rank statements
  (`rankAtLeast_of_covering`, `rankAtLeast_halfCanonical_of_covering`).
* `EnergyCovering.lean` — the energy (Dirichlet) form, cut sizes, the variational
  spectral gap, the Poincaré inequality, the easy direction of Cheeger's inequality
  and a lower bound for the covering radius of the Laplacian lattice in the energy
  metric.
* `Reduced.lean` — `q`-reduced divisors via a strictly superharmonic potential,
  **Riemann's theorem for graphs** (`deg D ≥ g ⇒ D` is equivalent to an effective
  divisor), Riemann's inequality `r(D) ≥ deg D − g`, and the **unconditional
  covering bound** `IsCoveringBound G g`.
* `ReducedUnique.lean` — **uniqueness of the `q`-reduced representative** in a
  divisor class (maximum principle for chip firing), reduction inside the effective
  cone, and the resulting **effectivity criterion**: `r(D) ≥ 0` if and only if the
  `q`-reduced form of `D` has a nonnegative number of chips at `q`.  Consequently
  reduction is a complete invariant of the divisor class
  (`linEquiv_iff_reduced_eq`), and a reduced divisor is subcritical away from `q`
  (`IsReduced.lt_degree`).
* `Dhar.lean` — **Dhar's burning algorithm**: the burning process stabilises after
  `#V` rounds, a legal firing set never burns, the unburnt set is the largest legal
  firing set, and `D` is `q`-reduced exactly when the whole graph burns
  (`isReduced_iff_burn_eq_univ`).  This turns the quantifier over all vertex sets in
  the definition of reducedness into an effective test.
* `Jacobian.lean` — **finiteness of the Jacobian**: the `q`-reduced divisors of a
  fixed degree form a finite, complete and irredundant set of representatives of the
  divisor classes of that degree, of size at most `∏_{v ≠ q} deg v`
  (`exists_reps`, `card_le_prod_degree`).
* `EnergyPath.lean` — the Cauchy–Schwarz bridge `(x u − x w)² ≤ dist(u,w) · E(x)`
  and the sup-norm bound `|x u| ≤ √(d · E(x))` for mean-zero vectors.
* `EnergyRadius.lean` — an **unconditional upper bound for the covering radius in
  the energy metric**: on a connected graph with degrees at most `Δ`, every
  degree-zero divisor lies within energy distance `2Δ³n` of the Laplacian lattice
  (`exists_energy_close`).  The proof shows that the Laplacian is onto the mean-zero
  hyperplane (`exists_mulVec_eq`, via Mathlib's description of its kernel) and then
  rounds coordinates, using the operator estimates `E(x) ≤ 2Δ‖x‖²` and
  `‖Lz‖² ≤ 2Δ E(z)`.  Combined with the bridge this gives unconditional `ℓ^∞`
  covering and Brill–Noether statements in terms of `Δ` and the diameter.
* `DiameterBound.lean` — ball growth in graphs of bounded degree and the Moore-type
  diameter lower bound `log_{k+1} n ≤ diam`.
* `CoveringBridge.lean` — the passage from an energy covering radius `ε` to the
  `ℓ^∞` covering bound `√(d ε)` and hence to Brill–Noether existence.

## What remains

1. **The lossiness of the covering mechanism.**  `rankAtLeast_of_covering` produces
   rank `r` only from `deg D ≥ n(ρ + r)`, because it forces *every* vertex to hold
   `ρ + r` chips simultaneously.  At the half-canonical degree `g − 1` this needs
   `ρ ≲ g/n − r`, i.e. `ρ` smaller than half the average degree, which no covering
   radius bound of the size predicted by the paper (`ρ ≈ √g`) can satisfy.  The
   paper's argument instead chooses the auxiliary effective divisor `E` adapted to
   the point of the lattice, and measures the distance in the energy norm rather
   than in `ℓ^∞`.  Formalising that refinement — a rank criterion of the shape
   "`deg D ≥ g − 1` and covering radius `≤ c√g` imply `r(D) ≳ √g`" — is the single
   most important missing step, and everything else below feeds into it.

2. **Baker–Norine Riemann–Roch.**  `r(D) − r(K − D) = deg D + 1 − g`.  With
   `Reduced.lean`, `ReducedUnique.lean` and `Dhar.lean` the reduced-divisor calculus
   is complete, so the missing ingredient is the combinatorics of acyclic
   orientations with a unique source: the non-special divisors of degree `g − 1` are
   exactly the classes `ν_σ`, and reversing `σ` realises `D ↦ K − D`.  This is what
   makes the half-canonical degree self-dual and hence the natural place to test the
   Brill–Noether conjecture: at `deg D = g − 1` Riemann's inequality gives nothing.

3. **Sharper covering radii.**  `Reduced.lean` gives `ρ ≤ g` in `ℓ^∞`, optimal in
   general (a tree of loops), and `EnergyRadius.lean` gives `ε ≤ 2Δ³n` in the energy
   metric with no use of expansion.  The paper's point is that expansion should
   force `ε` down to the order of `g`; proving this requires replacing the crude
   rounding argument of `EnergyRadius.lean` by a transference/counting argument for
   the Laplacian lattice which uses the spectral gap.

4. **The hard direction of Cheeger's inequality**, `λ₂ ≥ h²/(2Δ)`, i.e. the sweep-cut
   argument.  It is the analytic input that converts combinatorial expansion
   hypotheses (expanders, almost-Ramanujan graphs, random regular graphs) into the
   spectral gap used in item 3.

5. **Quantitative Brill–Noether for explicit families.**  With items 1, 3 and 4 one
   could formalise that `k`-regular graphs with a spectral gap bounded below satisfy
   `r(D) ≥ c√g` at `deg D = g − 1`, and the random graph statements of the paper.

6. **Reversal systems.**  The Moore-type bound in `DiameterBound.lean` is the generic
   ball-growth estimate; specialising it to the transition graphs of reversal
   systems (whose degrees are bounded by the number of allowed reversals) gives the
   logarithmic diameter lower bounds used as an application in the paper.

7. **Computability.**  `Dhar.lean` makes reducedness testable and `Jacobian.lean`
   bounds the number of classes, but the reduction *algorithm* itself (fire the
   unburnt set, repeat) is still obtained in `Reduced.lean` by minimising a
   potential rather than by a terminating recursion, and `reps` is defined with
   classical choice.  Turning these into executable definitions would allow
   machine-checked small-graph experiments of the kind recorded in
   `ComputationalEvidence.md`, in particular exact Baker–Norine ranks at the
   half-canonical degree.

# Future directions

## What is now proved

Two new self-contained files extend the conditional Hilbert-class-field interface of
`Catalog/NumberTheory/`, settling target 2 of the previous cycle (the Galois `p`-binomial count
for elementary abelian class groups).

### `Catalog/NumberTheory/SubspaceCounting.lean` (no dependencies beyond Mathlib)

Let `K` be a finite field with `q` elements and `V` a finite `K`-vector space of dimension `n`.

* `gaussBinom q n k` : the Gaussian binomial coefficient `∏_{i<k}(q^n-q^i) / ∏_{i<k}(q^k-q^i)`;
* `spanFiberEquiv` : the linearly independent `k`-tuples spanning a fixed `k`-dimensional
  subspace `W` are exactly the bases of `W`;
* `card_linearIndependent_eq_mul` : fibring the linearly independent `k`-tuples of `V` over
  their spans, `#{s : LI k-tuple} = #{W : dim W = k} · ∏_{i<k}(q^k-q^i)`;
* `card_submodule_finrank_mul` : `#{W : dim W = k} · ∏_{i<k}(q^k-q^i) = ∏_{i<k}(q^n-q^i)`;
* `card_submodule_finrank_eq_gaussBinom` : `#{W : dim W = k} = gaussBinom q n k` for `k ≤ n`;
* `card_submodule_finrank_pos`, `card_submodule_finrank_eq_zero` : the count is positive exactly
  in the range `k ≤ n`;
* `card_submodule_eq_sum_gaussBinom` : `#(subspaces of V) = ∑_{k ≤ n} gaussBinom q n k`
  (the Galois number, OEIS A006116 for `q = 2`);
* `card_submodule_finrank_le_sub`, `card_submodule_finrank_eq_card_submodule_finrank_sub` :
  duality — `W ↦ W^⊥` (dual annihilator, transported by a basis isomorphism `V* ≃ V`) is
  injective, whence there are as many `k`-dimensional as `(n-k)`-dimensional subspaces;
* `gaussBinom_symm`, `gaussBinom_pos` : consequences at `q = p` prime, obtained from the
  `(ZMod p)^n` model;
* `card_submodule_finrank_zmod`, `card_submodule_zmod` : the counts for `(ZMod p)^r`.

### `Catalog/NumberTheory/ElementaryAbelianClassField.lean`

For a Hilbert class field datum `e : Gal(H/K) ≃* Cl(𝒪_K)` together with an isomorphism
`E : Cl(𝒪_K) ≃* (ℤ/p)^r` (`p` prime):

* `classGroupSubmoduleOrderIso` : `Subgroup Cl(𝒪_K) ≃o Submodule (ZMod p) ((ZMod p)^r)`;
* `card_subgroup_eq_pow`, `index_eq_pow` : a subgroup corresponding to a `k`-dimensional
  subspace has order `p^k` and index `p^{r-k}`;
* `intermediateFieldSubmoduleEquiv` : intermediate fields of `H/K` ↔ subspaces of `(ZMod p)^r`;
* `card_intermediateField_eq_sum_gaussBinom` : **the datum has exactly `∑_{k≤r} binom(r,k)_p`
  intermediate fields**;
* `finrank_eq_pow_sub`, `finrank_eq_pow`, `finrank_classField_eq_pow` : degrees are the expected
  powers of `p`;
* `card_intermediateField_finrank_eq_gaussBinom` : **exactly `binom(r,k)_p` intermediate fields
  have degree `p^k` over `K`** (this is where `gaussBinom_symm` is used);
* `exists_intermediateField_finrank`, `exists_intermediateField_finrank_iff` : the degrees that
  occur are exactly `p^k`, `k ≤ r`;
* `sum_card_intermediateField_finrank` : the degreewise counts sum to the total count;
* explicit cases: `card_intermediateField_kleinFour` and `card_intermediateField_of_kleinFour`
  (`p = r = 2`: five intermediate fields, `card_quadratic_intermediateField_of_kleinFour`: three
  of them quadratic, `finrank_eq_one_or_two_or_four`), and
  `card_intermediateField_elementary_two_three` together with
  `card_intermediateField_finrank_two_three` (`p = 2, r = 3`: **sixteen** intermediate fields,
  with degree distribution `1, 7, 7, 1` in degrees `1, 2, 4, 8`).

The two falsifiable predictions of the previous cycle at `p = r = 2` (`5 = 1 + 3 + 1`) and at
`p = 2, r = 3` (`16 = 1 + 7 + 7 + 1`) are therefore both confirmed, as instances of a general
theorem rather than case analysis. All results are proved with no `sorry` and use only
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.

### `Catalog/Speculative/AutoResearch/KleinFourClassField.lean` (now complete)

The standalone Klein four case, which had been left with five unproved statements, is finished;
the file compiles with no `sorry` and its theorems use only `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`.  For a datum `e : Gal(H/K) ≃* Cl(𝒪_K)` together with `E : Cl(𝒪_K) ≃* V`, where
`V = ℤ/2 × ℤ/2`:

* `card_subgroup_V` : `V` has exactly five subgroups (from `subgroup_cases`);
* `index_comap_equiv` : transporting a subgroup of `V` back to the class group preserves index;
* `card_intermediateField_of_kleinFour` : the datum has exactly five intermediate fields,
  obtained from `HilbertClassFieldDescent.card_intermediateField_eq_card_subgroup` and
  `MulEquiv.mapSubgroup E`;
* `finrank_eq_one_or_two_or_four` : every intermediate field has degree `1`, `2` or `4` over `K`,
  from `HilbertClassFieldDescent.finrank_eq_index` and `index_cases`;
* `finrank_quadField` : the class field of `⟨x⟩` for `x ≠ 1` is quadratic over `K`;
* `quadField_injective` and `exists_three_quadratic_intermediateField` : the three subgroups of
  order two give three pairwise distinct quadratic intermediate fields;
* `intermediateField_eq_of_kleinFour` : conversely every intermediate field is `K`, `H`, or one
  of those three quadratic fields, so the degree multiset is exactly `{1, 2, 2, 2, 4}`.

This is the `p = r = 2` instance of the general count above, proved independently and by hand.

## Next targets

Each of the following is falsifiable: it is either a Lean statement that compiles and is proved,
or it fails for an explicit counterexample.

1. **General finite abelian class group.** Replace `(ℤ/p)^r` by an arbitrary finite abelian
   group `A`. The number of intermediate fields is the number of subgroups of `A`, which is
   multiplicative over the primary components; prove
   `Nat.card (Subgroup A) = ∏_p Nat.card (Subgroup A_p)` and, for `A_p = ⊕ ℤ/p^{λ_i}`, the
   Birkhoff–Hall count. Falsifiable already at `A = ℤ/4`, where the answer is `3`, versus
   `A = (ℤ/2)²`, where it is `5`.

2. **The `q`-Pascal recursion.** Prove
   `gaussBinom q (n+1) (k+1) = gaussBinom q n k + q^{k+1} * gaussBinom q n (k+1)` directly in ℕ,
   and deduce `gaussBinom_symm` for arbitrary `q > 1` (not only for prime `q`, where the present
   proof goes through the `(ZMod q)^n` model). Falsifiable at `q = 4, n = 2, k = 1`.

3. **Unconditional imaginary-quadratic instance.** For `K = ℚ(√-5)` construct
   `Nat.card (ClassGroup (𝓞 K)) = 2` and the datum `Gal(K(i)/K) ≃* Cl(𝒪_K)`, so that
   `card_intermediateField_eq_sum_gaussBinom` becomes an unconditional statement (`p = 2`,
   `r = 1`, two intermediate fields). Falsifiable: the class number must be `2`, not `1`.

4. **Frobenius compatibility of the Artin datum.** Demand that `e⁻¹` send the class of an
   unramified prime `𝔭` to `arithFrobAt 𝔭`, and prove that `𝔭` splits completely in `H` iff
   `[𝔭] = 1`. In the elementary abelian case this refines the counting above into a splitting
   law: the primes splitting completely in the degree-`p^k` class field of a subspace `W` are
   exactly those whose class lies in `W`.

5. **Genus theory.** For imaginary quadratic `K` with `t` prime discriminant divisors, prove
   `Nat.card (Cl ⧸ Cl²) = 2^{t-1}` and identify the corresponding class field as the genus
   field. Combined with the present count, when `Cl(𝒪_K)` is elementary abelian of rank `r` the
   genus field is the whole Hilbert class field and `r = t - 1`. Falsifiable at `K = ℚ(√-15)`,
   where the prediction is degree `2`.

# Future directions

The file `Applications/EML/ActivationMonotonicityTropicalBridge.lean` proves:

* the exact derivative and second-derivative formulas for the generalized EML
  activation `E_{a,b}(x) = a x + log(1 + e^{bx})`;
* strict convexity on all of `ℝ` for every `b ≠ 0` (`emlAct_strictConvexOn`);
* the sharp monotonicity criterion `StrictMono E_{a,b} ↔ 0 ≤ a` for `b > 0`
  (`emlAct_strictMono_iff`), with the failure for `a < 0` proved via the
  derivative limit at `−∞`;
* that log-sum-exp `x ⊕_b y = (1/b) log(e^{bx} + e^{by})` is exactly commutative,
  associative and distributive over `+`, with idempotency defect exactly
  `log 2 / b` (`lse_self`);
* the sharp sandwich `max x y < x ⊕_b y ≤ max x y + log 2 / b` and the
  resulting convergence to tropical (max-plus, resp. min-plus via Mathlib's
  `Tropical`) addition as `b → ∞`;
* the bridge theorem `eml_activation_tropical_bridge` tying the convex-analytic
  and tropical pictures together.

Natural continuations:

1. **`n`-ary and measure-theoretic log-sum-exp.** Replace the binary `⊕_b` by
   `(1/b) log ∑_{i<n} e^{b x_i}` and by `(1/b) log ∫ e^{b f} dμ`; the sandwich
   becomes `max ≤ · ≤ max + log n / b` (resp. essential supremum), giving
   `L^p → L^∞` style dequantization statements.

2. **Strict convexity as a function of two variables.** Prove that
   `(x,y) ↦ x ⊕_b y` is convex but not strictly convex, being affine along the
   diagonal `x = y` (`lse_self` already gives the diagonal restriction exactly);
   the tropical limit `max` is convex and affine on each of two half-planes.

3. **Tropical semiring structure as a Lean instance.** Endow `ℝ` with the
   `b`-deformed operations `(⊕_b, +)` as a genuine `Semiring` instance
   transported along `x ↦ e^{bx}` from `ℝ_{>0}`, and formalize the statement
   that these semirings converge (in the sense of Gromov–Hausdorff or of
   pointwise convergence of structure maps) to `Tropical ℝ`.

4. **Tropical polynomials from neural networks.** A ReLU network computes a
   tropical rational function; the `b`-smoothed network computes a
   log-sum-exp expression. Quantifying the uniform distance between a smoothed
   network of depth `d` and its tropical limit (an `O(d · log(width)/b)` bound)
   would extend the bridge theorem from one neuron to a whole architecture.

5. **Sharp monotonicity domains for other EML activations.** The same analysis
   applies to `x·σ(bx)` (Swish/SiLU), `x·tanh(log(1+e^{bx}))` (Mish) and
   `a x + (1/b) log cosh(bx)`; each has an exact parameter domain of
   monotonicity/convexity, and each degenerates to a piecewise-linear tropical
   expression as `b → ∞`.

6. **Rate optimality.** Prove that `log 2 / b` cannot be replaced by
   `c / b` with `c < log 2`, and study the second-order expansion
   `x ⊕_b y = max x y + (1/b) log(1 + e^{-b|x-y|})`.

# Future directions: Erdős–Rényi threshold phenomena

This cycle proved the **sharp connectivity threshold** of `G(n,p)` at `p = log n / n`
inside the catalog's elementary finite model
(`ErdosRenyi.mass` / `ErdosRenyi.Prob` on `Finset (Edge n)`):

* `ErdosRenyi.prob_connected_log_tendsto_zero` — for `0 < c < 1`,
  `P(G(n, c·log n/n) connected) → 0` (second moment on the isolated-vertex count);
* `ErdosRenyi.prob_connected_log_tendsto_one` — for `c > 1`,
  `P(G(n, c·log n/n) connected) → 1` (cut union bound + entropy/Stirling estimate);
* `ErdosRenyi.connectivity_sharp_threshold` — the two halves packaged together;
* `ErdosRenyi.isolated_vertex_sharp_threshold` — the companion sharp threshold for the
  existence of an isolated vertex (probability `→ 1` for `c < 1`, `→ 0` for `c > 1`).

Supporting reusable results: `prob_avoids` (all-absent probability `(1-p)^{|T|}`),
`expect_avoidCount` / `expect_avoidCount_sq` (exact first and second moments of a count
of avoided edge-blocks), `expect_isolated_count`, `expect_isolated_count_sq` and
`expect_isolated_count_factorial_two` (exact moments of the isolated-vertex count),
`variance_eq_sub`, `probZero_isolated_le` / `prob_connected_le` (the explicit Chebyshev
bound `1/(n(1-p)^{n-1}) + p/(1-p)`), `prob_disconnected_le` (cut union bound),
`card_cutEdges` (a cut has exactly `|S|·|Sᶜ|` potential edges), `choose_le_exp`
(`C(n,k) ≤ (e n/k)^k`).

The following conjectures are concrete and falsifiable next targets.

## C1. Poisson window at `p = (log n + c)/n`

**Conjecture.** For every `c ∈ ℝ`,
`Prob ((log n + c)/n) {s | (graphOf s).Connected} → exp(-exp(-c))`.

Falsifiable: a proof must in particular reproduce the value `e^{-1} ≈ 0.3679` at
`c = 0`, and any numerical simulation deviating from `e^{-e^{-c}}` refutes it.
The missing ingredient is a Poisson limit theorem (method of moments or Stein–Chen)
for the isolated-vertex count `I_n`, whose factorial moments in the present model are
exactly computable by the same block-avoidance technique as `expect_avoidCount_sq`:
`E[(I_n)_r] = n(n-1)⋯(n-r+1)·(1-p)^{r(n-1) - C(r,2)}`.  The case `r = 2` is now proved
(`expect_isolated_count_factorial_two`:
`E[I_n(I_n-1)] = n(n-1)(1-p)^{2n-3}`), so the remaining milestone is:

> **C1'.** The `r`-th factorial moment formula above for all `r`, whose combinatorial
> core is `|star(v_1) ∪ ⋯ ∪ star(v_r)| = r(n-1) - C(r,2)` for distinct vertices — a
> direct generalisation of `card_incident_union`.

## C2. Sharp threshold for minimum degree ≥ 1 versus connectivity coincide

**Conjecture.** With `p = c·log n/n` and `c > 1`,
`Prob p {s | (graphOf s).Connected} - Prob p {s | ∀ v, ∃ u, (graphOf s).Adj v u} → 0`;
i.e. above the threshold, *the only* obstruction to connectivity is an isolated vertex.

This strengthens the pair (`prob_exists_isolated_tendsto_zero`,
`prob_connected_log_tendsto_one`): the current proofs bound both quantities separately,
whereas the conjecture asserts the events differ with vanishing probability.  It is
falsified by exhibiting `c > 1` and a positive `ε` with a subsequence on which the gap
exceeds `ε`.  A proof should follow by refining `prob_disconnected_le` to cuts of size
`2 ≤ k ≤ n/2` only, whose total contribution is `O(n^{-δ})` for `δ = δ(c) > 0`.

## C3. Threshold for a fixed subgraph `H` at `n^{-1/m(H)}`

**Conjecture.** For a fixed graph `H` with `m(H) = max_{H' ⊆ H, v(H')>0} e(H')/v(H')`
and `p_n = ω(n) · n^{-1/m(H)}` with `ω → ∞`, the number of copies of `H` in `G(n,p_n)`
is positive with probability `→ 1`, while for `ω → 0` it is `0` a.a.s.

The `→ 0` half is already implied by `first_moment_threshold`; the `→ 1` half needs the
second-moment estimate `Var X = O((E X)^2 / Φ)` with `Φ = min_{H'} E[X_{H'}]`, which can
be assembled from `ErdosRenyi.secondMoment_subgraphCount` (exact overlap sum) plus
`subgraph_count_pos_whp`.  Falsifiable by a single `H` for which the claimed exponent
`1/m(H)` is wrong (e.g. by simulation for `H = K_4` with a pendant edge).

## C4. Giant component: quantitative subcritical bound

**Conjecture.** For `p = (1-ε)/n` with `0 < ε < 1` there is `A = A(ε)` such that
`Prob p {s | largestComponent s ≤ A · log n} → 1`, and the explicit choice
`A = 3/(ε - log(1+ε))` works.

The natural Lean route avoids branching processes entirely: a first-moment bound on the
number of *connected* vertex sets of size `k` — `C(n,k) k^{k-2} p^{k-1}` for trees —
combined with the cut machinery of `ErdosRenyiConnectivityUpper` (`cutEdges`,
`sum_over_small_sets`).  Falsifiable numerically: simulate `G(n,(1-ε)/n)` and check
whether the largest component exceeds `A log n` with non-vanishing frequency.

## C5. Monotonicity/sharpness of the connectivity probability in `c`

**Conjecture.** For each fixed `n ≥ 2` the map
`c ↦ Prob (c·log n/n) {s | (graphOf s).Connected}` is nondecreasing on `[0, n/log n]`.

This is a finite-`n` statement (an instance of Harris/FKG monotonicity for the increasing
event "connected"), and hence directly falsifiable by exact enumeration for small `n`.
Proving it in the present model requires a Harris-type coupling lemma for `mass`, which
does not yet exist in the catalog and would be reusable far beyond connectivity.

# Future Directions

Results of this cycle live in `Catalog/Combinatorics/ThreeQubitHyperdeterminant.lean`
(self-contained, `import Mathlib`, no `sorry`, axioms: `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`). Proved there: relative `SL(2)^{×3}` invariance of Cayley's
`2 × 2 × 2` hyperdeterminant, its permutation symmetry, its vanishing on biseparable
states, SLOCC inequivalence of GHZ and W, covariance and local-unitary invariance of the
one-tangle, the two-qubit pure-state identity `4 det ρ_A = C²`, CKW saturation on the
generalized GHZ and W families, and the monogamy bound `τ_ABC ≤ τ_{A|BC}` with its sharp
corollary `τ_ABC ≤ 1`.

Open directions building on this:

1. **Full CKW inequality.** Define the convex-roof squared concurrences `C_AB²`, `C_AC²`
   of the two-qubit reductions of a normalized pure three-qubit state and prove
   `C_AB² + C_AC² ≤ 4 det ρ_A`. The key missing ingredient is Wootters' formula for the
   concurrence of a rank-`≤ 2` two-qubit mixed state (eigenvalues of `ρ ρ̃`), which would
   also upgrade `residualTangle_le_oneTangleA` to the exact identity
   `τ_{A|BC} − C_AB² − C_AC² = 4 |Det ψ|`.

2. **GHZ normal form.** Prove the converse of `ghz_not_slocc_wState`: every tensor with
   `hyperdet ψ ≠ 0` is SLOCC equivalent to GHZ, and every genuinely entangled tensor with
   `hyperdet ψ = 0` is SLOCC equivalent to W. Together with the invariance results already
   available this would give the complete Dür–Vidal–Cirac classification of three-qubit
   SLOCC orbits.

3. **Equality analysis.** Characterize the tensors saturating `τ_ABC = τ_{A|BC}`. The
   proof given here reduces this to equality in the triangle inequality and in AM–GM for
   the six minors, so an explicit description of the extremal set should be within reach.

4. **Higher local dimension.** Extend `hyperdet_eq_minors` and the Cauchy–Binet identity
   to `2 × 2 × n` tensors, where the same slice-minor technique bounds the analogue of the
   residual tangle by the one-tangle.

# Affine subspace statistics in `𝔽₂ⁿ` — results and future directions

All formal results live in four files, which together compile with no `sorry` and use only
the standard axioms (`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`):

| file | contents |
|---|---|
| `Catalog/Applications/AffineSubspaceStats/AffineStats.lean` | the model, the parity bound `λ(d,s) ≤ 1/2` for odd `s` and its sharpness, `λ*(1,1) = 1/2`, the hyperplane computation, duality, disproofs |
| `Catalog/Applications/AffineSubspaceStats/CodimSubspace.lean` | the codimension-`m` and union-of-parallel-flats lower-bound constructions, and the exact criterion `\|F ∩ A\| = 2^{d-m} ⇔ the projected directions span` |
| `Catalog/Applications/AffineSubspaceStats/ExactProduct.lean` | the exact value `∏_{i<m}(1 - 2^{i-d})` of the construction's probability |
| `Catalog/Applications/AffineSubspaceStats/RandomConstruction.lean` | the random construction for `s = 1`: `λ*(d,1) ≥ (1-2^{-d})^{2^d-1} → e^{-1}`, and the strict comparison with the algebraic construction |

## The model

`λ*(d, s)` is the `n → ∞` limit of `max_{A ⊆ 𝔽₂ⁿ} P[|F ∩ A| = s]` over uniformly random
`d`-flats `F`. The formalisation samples an affine map instead of a flat: a base point `c`
and directions `v₀, …, v_{d-1}`, all uniform and independent, giving the cube
`{c + ∑ yᵢvᵢ : y ∈ 𝔽₂^d}` and the statistic `cnt A c v`. The directions are linearly
independent with probability `1 - O(2^{d-n})` (`card_indep_ge`), in which case the cube
*is* a `d`-flat, so the two models have the same `n → ∞` limits, while the cube model
supports clean finite counting arguments.

## What was proved

### Upper bounds and sharpness (`AffineStats.lean`)

**The parity bound.** For every `n`, every `d ≥ 1` and every `A ⊆ 𝔽₂ⁿ`,
`P[|F ∩ A| is odd] ≤ 1/2` (`oddProb_le_half`), hence `λ(d, s) ≤ 1/2` for every odd `s`
(`flatProb_le_half_of_odd`). The proof splits the `(d+1)`-cube into two parallel `d`-cubes
based at `c` and `c + u`; for fixed remaining directions the pair `(c, c+u)` is a pair of
independent uniform points, and the number of pairs landing in a symmetric difference is
`2m(2ⁿ - m) ≤ 2^{2n-1}`.

**The bound `1/2` is sharp.** Averaging over all `2^{2ⁿ}` subsets `A` (each
independent-direction cube meets exactly half of them oddly, `card_subsets_odd`) produces a
set with `P[odd] ≥ 1/2 - (2^{d+1}-1)/2^{n+1}` (`exists_oddProb_ge`), so
`max_A P[|F ∩ A| odd] → 1/2` (`tendsto_maxOddProb`).

**`λ*(1, 1) = 1/2` exactly** (`tendsto_maxFlatProb_one`).

**Disproofs / limits of the phenomena.**

* `exists_flatProb_gt_half`: the parity bound does not extend to even `s` — the hyperplane
  gives `P[|F ∩ A| = 2^{d}] = 1 - 2^{-(d+1)} > 1/2`. Oddness is exactly the right hypothesis.
* `flatProb_univ`: at `s = 2^d` the maximum is `1`, not `1 - 2^{-d}`; the formula
  `λ*(d, j·2^k) = 1 - 2^{-k}` requires `s < 2^d`.
* `maxOddProb_dim2_lt_half`: for `n = d = 2` the maximum is `3/8 < 1/2`, verified by kernel
  computation. Hence `1/2` is a genuine limit, never attained for these parameters.

### Lower-bound constructions (`CodimSubspace.lean`)

Let `π : 𝔽₂ⁿ → 𝔽₂^m` be the projection onto the first `m` coordinates (`m ≤ n`).

* `cnt_unionFlats`: if the projected directions `π(v₀), …, π(v_{d-1})` span `𝔽₂^m`, then for
  every `S ⊆ 𝔽₂^m` the cube meets `A = π⁻¹(S)` — a union of `|S|` parallel flats of
  codimension `m` — in exactly `|S|·2^{d-m}` points.
* `card_bad_dirs_le`: the projected directions fail to span for at most a `(2^m - 1)/2^d`
  fraction of the direction tuples (union bound over the `2^m - 1` nonzero functionals; for
  each of them the `d` directions must independently lie in a hyperplane).
* `flatProb_ge_of_cnt_of_surj`, `unionFlats_flatProb_ge`, `codimSub_flatProb_ge`: therefore
  `P[|F ∩ A| = |S|·2^{d-m}] ≥ 1 - (2^m - 1)/2^d`.
* `flatProb_pow_two_ge` and `exists_flatProb_mul_pow_two_ge`: with `m = d - k` this is the
  classical lower-bound construction, in the sharpened form
  `λ(d, j·2^k) ≥ 1 - 2^{-k} + 2^{-d}` for every `1 ≤ j ≤ 2^{d-k}` — in particular
  `λ*(d, j·2^k) ≥ 1 - 2^{-k}`.
* `surj_of_cnt`, `flatProb_codimSub_eq`: for `m ≤ d` the converse also holds, so the
  probability *equals* the fraction of spanning direction tuples.

### The exact value of the construction (`ExactProduct.lean`)

* `surj_iff_linearIndependent`: `y ↦ ∑ yᵢwᵢ` is onto `𝔽₂^m` iff the `m` transposed vectors
  of `𝔽₂^d` are linearly independent (proved through the annihilator argument
  `exists_orth_of_not_surjective`).
* `card_surj_tuples`: hence the number of spanning `d`-tuples in `𝔽₂^m` is
  `∏_{i<m}(2^d - 2^i)` (via Mathlib's `card_linearIndependent`).
* `card_surj_dirs`: the projection `𝔽₂ⁿ → 𝔽₂^m` is equi-fibred, so the count in `𝔽₂ⁿ`
  reduces to the count in `𝔽₂^m`.
* `flatProb_codimSub_prod`: **for all `m ≤ n`, `m ≤ d`,**
  `P[|F ∩ A| = 2^{d-m}] = ∏_{i<m}(1 - 2^{i-d})`, independently of `n`. With `k = d - m`
  this is `∏_{t=k+1}^{d}(1 - 2^{-t})`, the exact value of the classical construction; it is
  strictly larger than `1 - 2^{-k}` and consistent with the union bound above.
* `flatProb_one_eq_prod`: the case `s = 1` gives `λ*(d, 1) ≥ ∏_{i<d}(1 - 2^{i-d})`, which is
  `1/2` at `d = 1` and decreases to `∏_{t≥1}(1 - 2^{-t}) ≈ 0.2887…`.

### The random construction for `s = 1` (`RandomConstruction.lean`)

The optimal construction for `s = 1` is not algebraic but random: keep each point of `𝔽₂ⁿ`
independently with probability `p`, so that a `d`-flat (which has `2^d` points) is hit
exactly once with probability `2^d p (1-p)^{2^d-1}`, maximal at `p = 2^{-d}`.  This is
formalised as a pure counting argument — averaging over the `(m+1)^{2ⁿ}` colourings
`g : 𝔽₂ⁿ → Fin (m+1)` and taking `A = g⁻¹(0)`, which realises `p = 1/(m+1)` exactly.

* `card_exactly_one`: for a fixed `T ⊆ α`, exactly `|T| · m^{|T|-1} · (m+1)^{|α|-|T|}`
  colourings `α → Fin (m+1)` vanish at exactly one point of `T`.  (Proved by expanding the
  indicator of the event as a product of local indicators and exchanging `∑` and `∏`.)
* `card_colourings_cnt_one`: applied to the point set of a nondegenerate cube, whose size is
  `2^d`.
* `exists_colouring_hitSet_ge`: averaging over colourings, some `A = g⁻¹(0)` attains the
  average, which is the nondegenerate fraction of the parameter space times
  `2^d m^{2^d-1}/(m+1)^{2^d}`.
* `exists_flatProb_one_ge`: hence, for every `m` and every `n ≥ d`,
  `λ(d,1) ≥ (2^d m^{2^d-1}/(m+1)^{2^d})·(1 - (2^d-1)/2ⁿ)`.
* `exists_flatProb_one_ge_opt`, `maxFlatProb_one_ge_limit`: with `m + 1 = 2^d` this gives
  `λ*(d,1) ≥ (1 - 2^{-d})^{2^d-1}` (as a statement about all sufficiently large `n`).
* `random_beats_codimSub`: for `2`-flats and `n ≥ 5` the random construction *strictly*
  beats the algebraic one (`≥ 783/2048` versus exactly `3/8`), so the codimension-`d`
  subspace is not optimal for `s = 1`.
* `tendsto_randomBound_exp`: `(1 - 2^{-d})^{2^d-1} → e^{-1}` as `d → ∞`, so the lower bound
  for `λ*(d,1)` tends to `1/e`, well above the algebraic `∏_{t≥1}(1-2^{-t}) ≈ 0.2887…`.

## Future directions

1. **`v₂(s) = k` for `k ≥ 1`: the upper bound.** The paper's main theorem is
   `λ*(d, j2^k) ≤ 1 - 2^{-k} + O(2^{-3k/2})`. The recursion used here gives, conditionally
   on the remaining directions, `P[N ≡ 2^k mod 2^{k+1}] = ∑_r p_r p_{2^k - r}` (convolution
   on `ℤ/2^{k+1}`), which for a *fixed* direction tuple is not bounded by anything better
   than `1`; the parity case `k = 0` is special because `∑_r p_r p_{1-r} = 2p₀p₁ ≤ 1/2`
   pointwise. Extending beyond `k = 0` requires averaging over several direction vectors
   simultaneously (the four base points `c, c+u₁, c+u₂, c+u₁+u₂` are 3-wise but not 4-wise
   independent). Formalising even `λ*(d, 2j) ≤ 1/2 + o(1)` would be a substantial step.

2. **Optimality of the construction for `s = 2^k`.** The lower bound
   `∏_{t=k+1}^d(1 - 2^{-t})` is now known exactly; is it optimal among *all* `A`, i.e. is
   `λ*(d, 2^k)` equal to it, or does the union of `j` parallel flats (or some other family)
   do better? The upper bound `λ*(d, s) ≤ 1` is all that is currently formalised for even
   `s`; even `λ*(d, 2^k) < 1` for `k < d` is open in this development.

3. **`λ*(d, 1)` for `d ≥ 2`: the upper bound.** The lower half is now done:
   `maxFlatProb_one_ge_limit` gives `λ*(d,1) ≥ (1 - 2^{-d})^{2^d-1}`, whose limit is `e^{-1}`
   (`tendsto_randomBound_exp`).  What remains is the matching upper bound
   `λ*(d,1) ≤ (1 - 2^{-d})^{2^d-1}`, i.e. the optimality of the random construction.  For
   `d = 1` this is the parity bound `≤ 1/2` (`flatProb_le_half_of_odd`), which is tight; for
   `d ≥ 2` the parity bound only gives `1/2`, and closing the gap to `27/64` at `d = 2`
   needs a genuinely new argument (an entropy/convexity bound on the distribution of
   `|F ∩ A|` conditioned on the directions, rather than the two-point convolution used for
   parity).  Even a bound of the shape `λ*(d,1) ≤ 1/2 - c` for an explicit `c > 0` and
   `d ≥ 2` would be new here.

4. **Equality analysis for the parity bound.** Our proof shows equality forces
   `m = 2^{n-1}` for almost every direction tuple, i.e. the "odd set" of base points is
   perfectly balanced at every level. Characterising the near-extremal `A` (and giving an
   explicit, non-probabilistic family attaining `1/2 - o(1)`) is open here: the current
   sharpness proof is pure averaging and produces no explicit witness.

5. **Non-attainment in general.** `maxOddProb_dim2_lt_half` is a single finite check.
   Is `max_A P[|F ∩ A| odd] < 1/2` for *all* finite `n` whenever `d ≥ 2`, and what is the
   exact rate of convergence (our bound gives `1/2 - O(2^{d-n})`)?

6. **From cubes to flats.** `card_indep_ge` shows the two models differ by `O(2^{d-n})`, but
   the statement "`λ(d,s)` computed with flats equals `λ(d,s)` computed with cubes up to
   `O(2^{d-n})`" is not yet a single formal theorem; proving it would let every bound above
   be quoted directly in the flat model.

# Future directions

The files in `Bridges/` develop Joyal's combinatorial species as transport-of-structure
functors and connect them to generating series.  Everything listed below is fully proved:
`lake build` compiles the whole `Bridges` library, no file contains `sorry`, and every
headline theorem depends only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.

## What is formalised

| file | content |
|------|---------|
| `SpeciesAnalyticBridge.lean` | `Species` (functor on the groupoid of finite sets), the equivalence with functors `Core Type ⥤ Type`, sum/product/derivative, the species `0, 1, X, E, S`, the product rule `card_mul`, and `egf_mul`, `egf_add`, `egf_deriv`, `egf_set = exp`, `egf_perm·(1-X)=1`, `egf_eq_iff` |
| `SpeciesAnalyticBridgeExtras.lean` | powers of species, `egf_pow`, `card_set_pow = kⁿ`, `exp(X)^k = exp(kX)`, Leibniz/commutativity/associativity transferred back from `ℚ⟦X⟧`, and `ofSequence`: every sequence of naturals is the counting sequence of a species |
| `SpeciesUnlabelled.lean` | the `Sym(n)`-action coming from functoriality, unlabelled counts, the type generating series, and Burnside's lemma for species |
| `SpeciesPartitions.lean` | conjugacy classes of `Sym(n)` ↔ partitions of `n` (surjectivity of cycle type), `unlabelled S n = p(n)`, `∑_σ |C(σ)| = n!·p(n)` |
| `SpeciesIso.lean` | isomorphism of species, invariance of all invariants, the two-way correspondence with natural isomorphisms of the associated functors (`toNatIso` / `ofNatIso`), the semiring isomorphisms `+`-comm/assoc/unit, `·`-distributivity, `F·0 ≅ 0` |
| `SpeciesLinearOrders.lean` | linear orders vs permutations: equipotent (`egf L = egf S`) but **not isomorphic** |
| `SpeciesColourings.lean` | the species of `k`-colourings, `egf = exp(X)^k`, `tgf = 1/(1-X)^k`, unlabelled colourings = multisets (stars and bars), Burnside for colourings |
| `SpeciesCycleIndex.lean` | fixed colourings of `σ` number `k^{c(σ)}`, whence `∑_{σ∈Sym(n)} k^{c(σ)} = C(k+n-1,n)·n!` |
| `SpeciesPointing.lean` | the pointed species `F•`, the **natural isomorphism `F• ≅ X · F′`** (`pointIso`), the bridge theorem `egf (F•) = X · d/dX (egf F)`, and `|E•⋯•[n]| = nᵏ` for iterated pointing |
| `SpeciesDerangements.lean` | the species `D` of derangements, `card_derang = numDerangements`, the **species isomorphism `D · E ≅ S`** (`derangMulSetIso`), the identity `∑ₖ C(n,k)·D_k = n!`, the generating series `egf D · exp X · (1-X) = 1`, the alternating-sum formula and the limit `D_n/n! → e⁻¹` |
| `SpeciesDerangementsUnlabelled.lean` | a permutation is fixed-point-free iff every part of its cycle-type partition is ≥ 2; hence `unlabelled D n` counts the partitions of `n` without parts equal to `1`, and Burnside gives `∑_σ #{derangements commuting with σ} = n!·#{such partitions}` |
| `SpeciesCycles.lean` | the species `C` of cycles, `|C[n]| = (n-1)!` for `n ≥ 1`, `C′` equipotent with `L`, hence `(d/dX)(egf C)·(1-X) = 1` with zero constant term — i.e. `egf C = log(1/(1-X))` — and `tgf C = X/(1-X)` |
| `SpeciesComposition.lean` | **substitution of species** `F ∘ G`: the structure `Blocking A` (a partition of `A`, encoded by block indicators), its blocks, the composite species `Species.comp` with its functoriality laws, the decomposition of a blocking of `Option A` (`optionEquiv`) and of its blocks (`blockOptionEquiv`), `A ≃ Σ blocks, block`, `∑ block sizes = |A|`, invariance of block sizes under transport, `card_comp` (the sum-over-partitions counting formula), `card_comp_zero`, degenerate cases `F ∘ 0`, `F ∘ 1`, and `Iso.compCongr` (composition respects isomorphism) |
| `SpeciesExponentialFormula.lean` | the bijection `(E ∘ G)′[A] ≃ Σ_{S ⊆ A} G′[S] × (E ∘ G)[Aᶜ]` (`derivCompSetEquiv`), the recurrence `a_{n+1} = ∑ₖ C(n,k) g_{k+1} a_{n-k}`, the differential equation `(egf (E∘G))′ = (egf G)′ · egf (E∘G)`, uniqueness for `A′ = f·A`, and the **exponential formula in closed form** `egf (E ∘ G) = exp(egf G)` (`egf_comp_set`, with `egf_comp_set_sub_const` for general `G`); applications: partitions are counted by the **Bell numbers** (`card_partitions`, `card_blocking_eq_bell`, `egf_partitions = exp(exp X - 1)`, the Bell recurrence `bell_succ_choose`), the species isomorphism `E ∘ X ≅ E` (`compSetSingIso`: the only partition with singleton blocks is the discrete one), and **`E ∘ C` is counted by `n!`** — the cycle decomposition of permutations — whence `exp(log(1/(1-X))) = 1/(1-X)` |
| `SpeciesCyclesDerangements.lean` | the species `C₂` of cycles of length ≥ 2, `egf C₂ = egf C - X`, the differential equations `D′·(1-X) = X·D` and `(egf (E∘C₂))′·(1-X) = X·egf (E∘C₂)`, hence `egf (E ∘ C₂) = egf D` and **derangements are sets of long cycles**: `|(E ∘ C₂)[n]| = numDerangements n` |

## Notes on the encoding of composition

A partition of `A` is encoded as a `Blocking A`: a Boolean-valued relation `rel` with
`rel a a` and `rel a b → rel b = rel a`, so that `rel a` is the indicator of the block of
`a`.  Blocks are the indicators in the range of `rel`, and are automatically nonempty;
consequently `Species.comp F G` is Joyal's `F ∘ G₊`, the constant term of `G` playing no
role (this is why `egf_comp_set_sub_const` subtracts it).  The Boolean encoding was chosen
because transport along a bijection is then *definitionally* well behaved
(`p.map (Equiv.refl A) = p` holds by `rfl`), which is what makes the functoriality laws of
`comp` provable without dependent-transport gymnastics.

## Natural next steps

1. **Naturality for the exponential formula.**  `derivCompSetEquiv` is an isomorphism of
   structure sets for each `A`, so `(E ∘ G)′` and `G′ · (E ∘ G)` are equipotent; upgrading
   it to a `Species.Iso` requires checking naturality of a composite of `Equiv`
   combinators (one of which is `Equiv.ofBijective`).  Rebuilding `blockOptionEquiv` with
   an explicit inverse would be the first step.

2. **The cycle decomposition as a species isomorphism.**  `card_comp_set_cyc` proves
   `|(E ∘ C)[n]| = n!` analytically.  The bijection `S ≅ E ∘ C` itself (a permutation is
   the set of its cycles) is the natural next target; `blockSigmaEquiv` (a partition
   decomposes the underlying set) is the tool for transporting the cyclic structures.
   The same remark applies to `D ≅ E ∘ C₂`, proved here only at the level of counts.

3. **Unlabelled composites.**  `unlabelled (E ∘ E) n` should be the number of *integer*
   partitions `p(n)`.  What is missing is (i) the multiset of block sizes as a map to
   `Nat.Partition n` — `sum_card_elems` supplies the sum condition — and (ii) the fact
   that two blockings with the same size multiset are conjugate, for which one needs a
   size-preserving matching of block sets glued through `blockSigmaEquiv`.

4. **General composition `F ∘ G` and associativity.**  `card_comp` gives the counting
   formula for an arbitrary outer species; the analytic counterpart
   `egf (F ∘ G) = (egf F) ∘ (egf G)` (substitution of power series) needs a grading of
   composites by the number of blocks, which would also produce the Stirling numbers of
   the second kind as `|{p : Blocking (Fin n) // #blocks = k}|`.  Associativity
   `(F ∘ G) ∘ H ≅ F ∘ (G ∘ H)` is the other missing structural isomorphism.

5. **The cycle index series.**  `Species.cycleCount` and `Species.burnside` are the two
   halves of `Z_F(x₁,x₂,…) = (1/n!) ∑_σ |Fix F(σ)| x^{cycle type}`.  Formalising `Z_F`
   would unify `egf` (`x₁ = X`, `xᵢ = 0`) and `tgf` (`xᵢ = Xⁱ`) and give Pólya enumeration
   as a corollary of `burnside_colour`; `Z_C`, `Z_D` and now `Z_{E∘G}` are good tests.

6. **The analytic functor proper.**  Define `F̂(X) = ⨿ₙ F[n] ×_{Sym(n)} Xⁿ` as an
   endofunctor of `Type` and prove that `F ↦ F̂` is fully faithful onto the analytic
   functors (Joyal).  `Species.toFunctor`, `Iso.toNatIso` and `card_obj` are the starting
   points; with composition now available, the compatibility `\widehat{F ∘ G} = F̂ ∘ Ĝ`
   becomes statable.

7. **Weighted and multisort species.**  Replacing `Nat.card` by a weight in a commutative
   semiring turns `egf_mul` into the weighted product rule; multisort species give
   multivariate exponential generating series and inversion formulas.

8. **A `Species` semiring (and composition monoid) up to isomorphism.**  Quotienting by
   isomorphism would present `egf` as a semiring homomorphism `Species/≅ → ℚ⟦X⟧` and,
   using `Iso.compCongr`, would make substitution a well-defined monoid operation on the
   quotient with `X` as unit.

9. **`PowerSeries.log`.**  `SpeciesCycles.lean` states `egf C = log(1/(1-X))` only through
   its derivative.  With `Mathlib`'s `PowerSeries.subst` now used here for `exp`, adding
   `log` (and `exp (log f) = f`) would let `egf C` and `egf D` be stated in closed form;
   `exp_subst_egf_cyc` is the special case proved combinatorially in this project.

10. **More separating invariants.**  `linOrd_not_iso_perm` shows `egf` does not determine
    a species.  Does `tgf` together with `egf` determine it?  (No — the cycle index series
    is strictly finer; explicit counterexamples would be a nice addition.)
